background.definition: Silicosis is an irreversible lung disease caused by inhalation of dust particles containing free crystalline silica.

list.listitem: At least 1.7 million US workers are exposed to respirable crystalline silica in a variety of industries and occupations.
Patients with silicosis are at an increased risk for lung cancer and pulmonary tuberculosis.
There may also be an association with systemic lupus erythematosis.
Exposure to silica dust is most commonly seen in occupations involving construction; mining and quarrying; metal working; and manufacturing of nonmetallic products, such as ceramics or glass.
A cohort study of 30,697 Chinese workers found that even low levels of silica dust exposure (below permissible limits) were associated with a significant increase in the lifetime risk of silicosis.
Inhalation of the crystalline (unbound) form of silica leads to silicosis.
An important contemporary cause is in workers exposed to engineered or artificial stone. It closely mimics disease caused by silica.
A systematic review of 8 studies supports reducing the permissible limit from 0.1 mg/m3 to 0.05 mg/m3.

Inhaled silica particles are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, causing the release of cytokines, growth factors, and oxidants that stimulate inflammation, synthesis of collagen, and lead to fibrosis. The fibrotic silica is later released into the interstitial tissue surrounding the small bronchioles, forming a silicotic nodule.
In addition, silica has been shown to directly stimulate human lung fibroblasts to produce inflammatory enzymes and prostaglandins.
The silicotic nodule has a classic onion-skin appearance.

There are 5 subtypes of silicosis, based primarily on exposure history and degree of symptoms: Chronic silicosis results from long-term exposure (20+ years) to silica dust in smaller amounts. Accelerated silicosis occurs after a shorter period of exposure (5-15 years) to larger amounts of silica dust. Complicated silicosis is the advanced form of chronic and accelerated silicosis in which patients often become symptomatic from progression of pleural disease. Acute silicosis occurs after short-term exposure to very large amounts of silica, which causes inflamed lung tissue and decreased oxygenation in a more acute setting. Progressive massive fibrosis is an advanced form of complicated silicosis in which silicotic nodules combine to form large fibrotic masses in the upper lung zones. The patient, therefore, experiences worsened dyspnea.
Silicosis is prevented by avoiding inhalation of dust containing free crystalline silica. C

Workers should use half-facepiece particulate respirators with N95 or better filters for airborne exposures to crystalline silica at concentrations less than or equal to 0.5 mg per cubic meter to help prevent silicosis; higher levels of exposure require additional measures. C

Employers should provide appropriate information to exposed workers regarding hazards; effective means for decreasing exposure through ventilation, dust suppression, and substitution; and proper protective equipment and clothing to help prevent silicosis. C
Workers exposed to silica should undergo annual screening including a physical, chest x-ray, and pulmonary function tests. C
Patients with silicosis should be screened for tuberculosis. B
Immunize against pneumococcal pneumonia and recommend an annual influenza vaccination. A
The presentation of silicosis can range from asymptomatic to severe dyspnea to respiratory failure depending on the subtype or phase of the disease. C

Silicosis is diagnosed based on history of exposure to silica with associated chest x-ray or CT scan findings (usually nodular changes in the upper lung zones and uniformly calcified mediastinal lymphadenopathy). C
High-resolution CT is more sensitive in detecting lung parenchymal changes of silicosis than radiography and can have additional value in distinguishing silicosis from other pulmonary diseases. B
Pulmonary function tests and ABGs are more useful for assessing progression of disease rather than the initial silicosis diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Chest x-ray shows diffuse infiltrates predominantly at bases; asbestos exposure
Often indistinguishable when exposure history is unclear without tissue biopsy
Noncalcified, well-defined lung nodules on CT or, if unclear, tissue biopsy
In acute phase, symptoms appear within hours of exposure; in chronic cases, CT shows patchy fibrosis
Chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar infiltrates; commonly with dermatologic, cardiac, or ocular findings
Tissue biopsy when suspected; PET scan can sometimes be helpful

list.listitem: Silicosis should be suspected in patients with a history of occupational exposure to silica. The risk is higher with more intensive levels of exposure and longer duration. In gold miners, risk is highest among those doing underground work.
Symptoms and physical examination findings will vary based on the type of silicosis:
Chronic silicosis: Patients are commonly asymptomatic since nodules and lymphadenopathy develop over time and often do not compromise lung volumes.

Complicated silicosis: Patients develop dyspnea on exertion that progresses to dyspnea at rest and often to productive cough. Examination reveals diminished breath sounds that worsen as the disorder progresses, along with signs of pulmonary consolidation, pulmonary hypertension, and respiratory failure with or without right ventricular heart failure (advanced disease).
Accelerated silicosis: Complicated (symptomatic) silicosis develops much more quickly in patients with accelerated silicosis despite the decreased duration of exposure.

Acute silicosis: History and physical examination reveals rapid progression of dyspnea, fatigue, and weight loss along with bilateral crackles throughout the lung fields. Respiratory failure also develops more quickly.
Progressive massive fibrosis: Patients experience similar symptoms as those with complicated silicosis although shortness of breath is often more severe because of more extensive lung involvement.
In patients with silica exposure, chest x-ray is typically performed first to look for silicosis (see below).

High-resolution CT is more sensitive than radiography in detecting lung parenchymal changes suggestive of silicosis and therefore may be of greater value than chest x-ray for patients in whom silicosis is suspected.

CT can also help distinguish silicosis from other pulmonary diseases since uniformly calcified and hyperdense mediastinal lymph nodes (seen on CT) are common in silicosis. Qualitative and quantitative CT parameters can also be used as indirect measures of functional impairment in silicosis.
Other tests, such as pulmonary function tests and ABGs, are of little value for diagnosis but can be helpful in assessing the progression of disease.

A diagnostic case-control study in 121 Indian patients found that levels of club cell protein 16 (CC16) are decreased in patients with silicosis: mean 4.7 ng/ml in advanced disease, 10.2 ng/ml in moderate disease, and 16.7 ng/ml in healthy controls. This was confirmed by a similar Thai study.

Chest x-ray and/or CT findings can also help distinguish between the types of silicosis: Chronic silicosis: Chest x-ray and CT usually reveal multiple small (1-3 mm) nodules in the upper lung fields with enlarged and calcified mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. Accelerated silicosis: Chest x-ray and CT findings are similar to chronic silicosis but with an accelerated disease course. Complicated silicosis: Chest x-ray and CT show progressive fibrosis with increased pleural findings, as well as a reduction of lung volumes, also evident on pulmonary function tests. Progressive massive fibrosis: Chest x-ray and CT shows larger (>10 mm) opacities often in the upper lungs bilaterally with chronic silicosis findings throughout.
Suspect silicosis in patients with dyspnea and a history of silica exposure.
Begin with chest x-ray; most patients will require CT to confirm the diagnosis.
Inhaled and oral steroids are used in selected patients, but good clinical trials are lacking.
Avoiding all sources of occupational exposure is central to therapy of silicosis.B
Although there is no curative treatment for silicosis, oxygen therapy, bronchodilators, antitussives, and inhaled corticosteroids can be helpful in the management of silicosis. B
Patients with more severe or end-stage disease should be evaluated for lung transplant.B
Treat patients with concurrent silicosis and tuberculosis with a longer course of antituberculosis chemotherapy. B
No treatment has been found to prevent or cure silicosis.
Inhaled corticosteroids are somewhat helpful in the management of patients with chronic silicosis.
Sometimes oral corticosteroids are used to treat acute and accelerated silicosis, although clinical trials are lacking.
Inhaled bronchodilators, antitussives, and oxygen therapy can be used to treat symptoms and hypoxia associated with silicosis.

Patients with silicosis and tuberculosis should receive appropriate multiple drug therapy according to current treatment guidelines. Because patients with silicosis respond poorly to antituberculosis chemotherapy, they should receive a longer course of treatment.
Aluminum citrate has shown some benefit in retarding the dust-induced fibrosis and decreasing the morbidity of silicosis.
Lung lavage is sometimes used to treat silicosis (more commonly in patients with acute silicosis).
A lung transplant is sometimes considered in patients with end-stage silicosis and without other significant comorbid conditions.
Remove patients from further exposure to silica and other lung irritants, occupational and otherwise.
Advise patients who smoke to quit.
Chronic silicosis may be asymptomatic and remain stable for many years both clinically and radiographically. C
Patients with complicated silicosis typically have gradual worsening of symptoms and lung function with increasing disability. C
Patients with acute, accelerated, and progressive massive fibrosis subtypes often progress rapidly to severe respiratory impairment. C
Patients with silicosis have an increased risk of lung cancer (relative risk (RR) = 3.6; 95% CI, 1.4-8.9). B
Patients with silica exposure in the absence of silicosis may be at an increased risk for lung cancer, but this risk is less than those with silicosis and not demonstrated through all studies.
Cigarette smoking strongly increases the lung cancer risk in silicotic patients (RR 4.47; 95% CI, 3.17-6.30).
Patients with silicosis have an increased risk of developing tuberculosis compared with healthy control patients (RR 2.8-3.9 times higher, depending on the severity of the silicosis). B
